source.title: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral
source.attribution: Francis Bacon, The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral, Project Gutenberg, public domain

cards.title: Plain dealing is the honour of a person; a little falsehood cheapens the whole
cards.body:
Bacon admits that even people who cut corners know, deep down, that straightforward dealing is what makes a person admirable. He compares mixing lies into your dealings to mixing cheap metal into gold coins: the coin may be easier to work with, but it is worth less.

The same is true of small dishonesties today. A padded CV line, an invented excuse to a colleague or a 'quick fib' to smooth things over can make life easier for a moment. Over time they lower the value of everything else you say, because people can no longer take your word at face value.
cards.quote: clear, and round dealing, is the honor of man's nature; and that mixture of falsehoods, is like alloy in coin of gold and silver, which may make the metal work the better, but it embaseth it.
cards.apply_it: Notice the next small excuse you are tempted to make this week. Try giving the plain reason instead and see what actually happens.

quiz.question: What does Bacon compare falsehood in everyday dealings to?
options: Cheap metal mixed into gold coins
A mask worn at a party
quiz.explanation: Like alloy in a gold coin, a lie may make things 'work better' for a while, but it lowers the worth of the whole.

cards.title: Passing doubts do little harm; the false idea you let settle in does the damage
cards.body:
Bacon makes a careful distinction. A wild idea that passes through your mind, like a story or a daydream, does little harm. The trouble comes from the false belief that sinks in and settles, until you stop noticing it is there and start acting on it.

This is a useful test for modern information overload. You will hear rumours, half-truths and flattering stories about yourself every day. You cannot stop them arriving. What you can do is notice which ones you have quietly started to treat as fact, and check them before they become part of how you see the world.
cards.quote: it is not the lie that passeth through the mind, but the lie that sinketh in, and settleth in it, that doth the hurt
cards.apply_it: Write down one belief you hold firmly but have never checked. Spend ten minutes looking for the best evidence against it.

quiz.question: According to Bacon, which kind of falsehood does the real harm?
options: The one that passes quickly through the mind
The one that sinks in and settles
quiz.explanation: A passing fancy does little damage. The lie that settles in the mind and goes unexamined is what hurts.

cards.title: Much of what frightens us about death is the scenery around it
cards.body:
Bacon notices that people fear death the way children fear the dark, and that the fear grows with the stories told about it. He quotes an old saying that the ceremony of death frightens more than death itself: the sickroom, the weeping, the black clothes and the funeral rites.

If you are facing a loss, or the fear of one, it may help to gently separate the two. The rituals and images can feel overwhelming, and that is natural. Bacon also offers a quieter thought: dying is as natural as being born. Neither makes grief smaller, but it can make the fear a little less lonely and a little less large.
cards.quote: It is as natural to die, as to be born; and to a little infant, perhaps, the one is as painful, as the other.
cards.apply_it: If fear of death or loss weighs on you, try naming one specific thing you fear about it, and share that with someone you trust.

quiz.question: What does Bacon say makes death seem more terrible?
options: The surrounding signs: weeping, mourning clothes and funerals
quiz.explanation: He quotes the saying that the pomp of death frightens more than death itself.

cards.title: Getting even makes you equal to the person who hurt you; letting it go puts you above
cards.body:
Bacon calls revenge 'a kind of wild justice'. It feels fair, but it has no limits and no referee. His sharper point is about status: when you take revenge, you are only level with your enemy. When you let the offence pass, you are the bigger person.

He adds a calming thought. Most people who wrong us are not doing it for the pleasure of hurting; they are chasing their own gain or comfort. Seen that way, the injury is less personal. Why be furious with someone for loving themselves more than they love you?
cards.quote: Certainly, in taking revenge, a man is but even with his enemy; but in passing it over, he is superior; for it is a prince's part to pardon.
cards.apply_it: Think of one small grudge you are carrying. Ask: what was this person really trying to get for themselves? Then decide if it is worth keeping.

quiz.question: Why does Bacon say most people do us wrong?
options: To gain profit, pleasure or honour for themselves
quiz.explanation: He argues no one does wrong for its own sake, so there is little reason to take it so personally.

cards.title: Planning revenge keeps your own wound open
cards.body:
After being hurt, especially by someone close, it is tempting to replay the injury and imagine ways to make them feel it too. Bacon has a simple warning: the person who keeps studying revenge keeps their own wounds fresh, when those wounds would otherwise heal.

This is not about pretending the hurt did not happen. It is about noticing where your attention goes. Every time you rehearse the scene or check up on them, the wound reopens. Turning your attention toward the present and the future is not letting them off the hook; it is letting yourself heal.
cards.quote: This is certain, that a man that studieth revenge, keeps his own wounds green, which otherwise would heal, and do well.
cards.apply_it: When the urge comes to replay an old hurt or check on the person, try a different action for five minutes: a walk, a call to a friend, a page of writing.

quiz.question: What does Bacon say happens to someone who dwells on revenge?
options: They keep their own wounds fresh
quiz.explanation: Studying revenge keeps wounds 'green' that would otherwise heal on their own.

cards.title: Hard times reveal strengths that easy times never test
cards.body:
Bacon says each season of life has its own virtue. In good times, the virtue to practise is moderation. In hard times, it is fortitude, the steady courage to keep going, and he calls that the more heroic of the two.

He uses a lovely image: good character is like a fragrant herb or incense, which gives off its best scent when it is crushed or burned. Comfortable times tend to expose our weaknesses, while difficulty often brings out qualities we did not know we had. That does not make suffering good, but it means it is not wasted.
cards.quote: Certainly virtue is like precious odors, most fragrant when they are incensed, or crushed: for prosperity doth best discover vice, but adversity doth best discover virtue.
cards.apply_it: Recall one difficult period you came through. Write down one strength it showed you that you did not know you had.

quiz.question: Which virtue does Bacon link with adversity?
quiz.explanation: Temperance is the virtue of prosperity; fortitude, the more heroic one, belongs to adversity.

cards.title: Even dark seasons hold small comforts, and they shine brighter there
cards.body:
Bacon offers a gentle balance. Good times are not free of fears and worries, and hard times are not without comforts and hopes. He points to embroidery: bright work stitched on a dark background is more pleasing to the eye than dark work on a light one.

In grief or a long struggle, you are not asked to feel cheerful. But small bright things, a kind message, a good meal, a moment of laughter, can stand out more clearly against the dark. Letting yourself notice them is not a betrayal of your sorrow. It is part of how people carry it.
cards.quote: Prosperity is not without many fears and distastes; and adversity is not without comforts and hopes.
cards.apply_it: Tonight, note one small comfort from today, however tiny. Keep the list for a week if it helps.

quiz.question: What image does Bacon use for comfort within hardship?
options: A ship in a calm harbour
A candle in an empty room
Bright embroidery on a dark, solemn background
quiz.explanation: He says lively work on a sad, solemn ground pleases the eye more than dark work on a light ground.

cards.title: Parents carry joys and fears they rarely say out loud
cards.body:
Bacon opens his essay on families with a tender observation. The joys of parents are private, and so are their griefs and fears. They often cannot put the joy into words, and they will not speak about the worries.

He also notes that children sweeten hard work but can make misfortunes feel more bitter, because there is more at stake. If you are a parent, it may help to know this hidden load is normal and worth sharing with a partner or friend. If you are a grown child, it is a reminder that your parents probably felt far more than they ever said.
cards.quote: THE joys of parents are secret; and so are their griefs and fears. They cannot utter the one; nor they will not utter the other.
cards.apply_it: If you are a parent, tell one trusted person about a worry you usually keep to yourself. If you are a grown child, ask a parent about a time they were proud of you.

quiz.question: What does Bacon say about parents' griefs and fears?
options: They pass them on to their children
quiz.explanation: Parents' joys are secret 'and so are their griefs and fears'; they will not speak them.

cards.title: Watch for the child in the middle who quietly gets forgotten
cards.body:
Bacon observed a pattern in large families: the eldest one or two get respect and responsibility, the youngest gets spoiled, and the children in the middle are, as he puts it, almost forgotten. Yet those overlooked children often turn out the best.

You do not need a big family to see the risk. In any family, attention tends to flow to the child who is loudest, newest or most in need. Fair love is not about identical treatment, but it does mean checking that no child is fading into the background just because they are easy to manage.
cards.quote: A man shall see, where there is a house full of children, one or two of the eldest respected, and the youngest made wantons; but in the midst, some that are as it were forgotten, who many times, nevertheless, prove the best.
cards.apply_it: This week, plan ten minutes of one-to-one time with the child who asks for the least attention.

quiz.question: In Bacon's observation, which children are often forgotten?
quiz.explanation: The eldest are respected and the youngest indulged, while the middle ones are overlooked, though they often prove the best.

cards.title: Stirring up rivalry between siblings can split a family for life
cards.body:
Bacon calls it a foolish habit, shared by parents, teachers and others, to breed competition between brothers and sisters while they are young. It may seem like a way to motivate children, but he saw that it often turns into lasting conflict once they are adults, troubling the whole family.

Comparisons like 'why can't you be more like your sister?' plant exactly this seed. Children can be encouraged to grow without being set against each other. Praise each child against their own progress, and help them cheer for one another instead.
cards.quote: Men have a foolish manner (both parents and schoolmasters and servants) in creating and breeding an emulation between brothers, during childhood, which many times sorteth to discord when they are men, and disturbeth families.
cards.apply_it: Catch yourself the next time you compare one child to another. Rephrase it as a comparison with that child's own past effort.

quiz.question: What does Bacon say childhood rivalry between siblings often leads to?
options: Discord when they are grown up
quiz.explanation: Bred rivalry 'many times sorteth to discord when they are men, and disturbeth families'.

cards.title: Family life is a daily school in tenderness
cards.body:
Bacon weighs the single life against married life fairly. Single people, he says, are often freer, and can be generous with their time and money. But he also observes that a spouse and children are 'a kind of discipline of humanity'. Living with people you love calls on your tenderness every day, and so keeps it in practice.

The point applies to any committed relationship. Its daily demands, patience at the end of a long day, care when someone is ill, compromise over small things, are not only costs. They are the training that makes us kinder.
cards.quote: Certainly wife and children are a kind of discipline of humanity
cards.apply_it: Think of one daily demand of your closest relationship that annoys you. Ask what quality it might be training in you.

quiz.question: Why does Bacon call family 'a kind of discipline of humanity'?
options: Because it constantly calls on our tenderness
Because it keeps people at home
quiz.explanation: He notes that people whose tenderness is not often called upon can grow harder; family keeps it in use.

cards.title: Envy is a wanderer: the more you watch others' lives, the more you envy
cards.body:
Bacon noticed that busy, nosy people are usually envious. Someone who keeps track of everyone else's affairs is not doing it for practical reasons; they get a kind of entertainment from watching other people's fortunes. And someone who minds their own business finds little to envy.

His phrase for it is memorable: envy walks the streets and never stays at home. Today the streets include our phones. Endless scrolling through other people's highlights is exactly the 'gadding' Bacon describes. Bringing your attention back home, to your own work and people, quietly starves envy of its food.
cards.quote: For envy is a gadding passion, and walketh the streets, and doth not keep home
cards.apply_it: Notice which accounts or conversations leave you feeling envious. Mute or step back from one of them for a week.

quiz.question: According to Bacon, who finds the least matter for envy?
options: Those who mind their own business
quiz.explanation: Envy 'gads' about in other people's affairs; whoever minds their own business finds little to envy.

cards.title: Envy bites hardest among siblings, old friends and colleagues
cards.body:
Bacon points out that we rarely envy distant celebrities as much as people close to us. Relatives, coworkers and those we grew up with are the most likely to feel envy when one of them rises. Their success seems to point a finger at our own situation, reminds us of it more often, and gets talked about by others.

Knowing this can help on both sides. If a friend's promotion stings, that is a common human reaction, not proof you are a bad person. And if you are the one who rose, a little humility and warmth toward old companions goes a long way.
cards.quote: Lastly, near kinsfolks, and fellows in office, and those that have been bred together, are more apt to envy their equals, when they are raised.
cards.apply_it: Next time a peer shares good news, congratulate them specifically and sincerely, even if part of you feels a pang.

quiz.question: Who, according to Bacon, is most likely to envy someone who rises?
options: Relatives, colleagues and those raised alongside them
quiz.explanation: Near kin, fellow workers and those bred together are most apt to envy an equal who is raised.

cards.title: Married love builds, friendly love perfects, and mere desire corrupts
cards.body:
Bacon is famously wary of passionate, all-consuming love. He thought it clouded judgment and could pull people away from their responsibilities. But he did not dismiss love itself. He ends his essay by sorting it into kinds.

Committed, married love, he says, makes humankind, building families and futures. Friendly love, the affection of companions, makes us better people. Love that is only lust or self-indulgence degrades us. In modern terms, a strong relationship needs more than chemistry: it needs commitment and real friendship too.
cards.quote: Nuptial love maketh mankind; friendly love perfecteth it; but wanton love corrupteth, and embaseth it.
cards.apply_it: Ask yourself honestly: is there real friendship in your relationship, beyond attraction? Name one way to strengthen it this week.

quiz.question: Which kind of love does Bacon say 'perfecteth' mankind?
quiz.explanation: Nuptial love makes mankind, friendly love perfects it, and wanton love corrupts it.

cards.title: Love that has nowhere to land can spread out to many
cards.body:
Bacon believed people have a deep, built-in pull toward loving others. If that love is not spent on one person or a few, it naturally spreads toward many, and makes people more humane and generous.

After a breakup or the end of a relationship, it can feel as if all that love has nowhere to go. Bacon's idea offers a gentle possibility. Your capacity to care has not disappeared. For a while it may flow to friends, family, community or causes, and that is not a lesser kind of love. It keeps your heart open while it heals.
cards.quote: There is in man's nature, a secret inclination and motion, towards love of others, which if it be not spent upon some one or a few, doth naturally spread itself towards many, and maketh men become humane and charitable
cards.apply_it: Choose one small act of care for someone outside your usual circle this week: a message, a visit, an hour volunteering.

quiz.question: What happens, in Bacon's view, to love that is not spent on one or a few people?
options: It spreads toward many and makes people kinder
quiz.explanation: He says it 'doth naturally spread itself towards many, and maketh men become humane and charitable'.

cards.title: Seeking power often means trading away your freedom
cards.body:
Bacon, who rose to the highest offices in England, writes about high position from the inside. People in great places, he says, serve three masters: the state, their reputation and their work. They lose freedom over their time, their actions and even themselves.

He finds it strange that people chase power and lose liberty, or seek control over others and lose control of themselves. He adds that busy great people rarely find time to care for their health, of body or mind. Before reaching for the next promotion, it is worth asking what you will give up to get it.
cards.quote: It is a strange desire, to seek power and to lose liberty: or to seek power over others, and to lose power over a man's self.
cards.apply_it: Before your next big career step, list what it will cost you in time, health and freedom, not just what it will give you.

quiz.question: Which three things does Bacon say people in high positions serve?
quiz.explanation: Men in great place are 'thrice servants': of the sovereign or state, of fame, and of business.

cards.title: Be firm if you must, but never rough: severity breeds fear, roughness breeds hate
cards.body:
Bacon lists four vices of people in authority: delays, corruption, roughness and being too easily swayed. On roughness he is sharp. It is a needless cause of resentment. Strictness may make people fear you, but harshness makes them hate you. Even when correcting someone, he says, a leader should be serious rather than mocking.

For anyone managing a team or a household, this is practical. You can hold high standards and give hard feedback. What turns people against you is sarcasm, belittling and public humiliation. Correct the work, not the person's dignity.
cards.quote: severity breedeth fear, but roughness breedeth hate. Even reproofs from authority, ought to be grave, and not taunting.
cards.apply_it: Before giving your next piece of critical feedback, strip out any sarcasm or jokes at the person's expense.

quiz.question: According to Bacon, what does roughness in a leader produce?
quiz.explanation: Severity breeds fear, but roughness breeds hate; reproofs should be grave, not taunting.

cards.title: Bold people are poor planners but great doers; use them that way
cards.body:
Bacon admits boldness wins people over, often more than wisdom. But he notes it keeps promises badly, because boldness is blind: it does not see dangers.

His advice is to put it in the right place. When deciding, it is good to see every danger. When acting, it is good not to be distracted by them unless they are very serious. So bold people make excellent seconds who carry out a plan, but should not be the ones who make it. In a modern team, that might mean pairing your fearless doer with a careful planner.
cards.quote: This is well to be weighed; that boldness is ever blind; for it seeth not danger, and inconveniences. Therefore it is ill in counsel, good in execution
cards.apply_it: On your next project, separate the planning stage from the doing stage. Who on your team is best suited to each?

quiz.question: Where does Bacon say boldness is most useful?
quiz.explanation: Because boldness does not see danger, it is 'ill in counsel, good in execution'.

cards.title: Be good to people without becoming a prisoner of their moods
cards.body:
Bacon calls goodness, real care for other people's welfare, the greatest of all virtues. But he warns about its counterfeit. Wanting to help people is not the same as needing to please them. If you become a slave to their expressions and whims, he says, that is just softness, and it takes an honest mind prisoner.

This is the line between kindness and people-pleasing. Kindness asks what is truly good for someone. People-pleasing asks how to avoid their frown. You can be generous and still say no.
cards.quote: Seek the good of other men, but be not in bondage to their faces or fancies; for that is but facility, or softness; which taketh an honest mind prisoner.
cards.apply_it: Think of a recent yes you regret. Ask: was I doing what was good for them, or avoiding their disappointment?

quiz.question: What does Bacon warn against in being good to others?
options: Being in bondage to their faces or fancies
quiz.explanation: Seeking others' good is the goal; being ruled by their moods and whims is mere softness.

cards.title: Learn a bit of the language before you go, and keep a travel journal
cards.body:
For Bacon, travel is education for the young and experience for the old. But he has firm advice for making it count. If you arrive somewhere without any of the language, you have gone to school, not travelled: you will spend your time just coping.

He also found it odd that sailors kept diaries at sea, where there is nothing but sky and water, while land travellers who saw so much wrote nothing down. So learn a few phrases before you leave, go with someone or something that knows the place, and keep notes on what you see.
cards.quote: He that travelleth into a country, before he hath some entrance into the language, goeth to school, and not to travel.
cards.apply_it: Before your next trip, learn twenty useful phrases and pack a small notebook for one line of observations each day.

quiz.question: What did Bacon find strange about travellers in his day?
options: They kept diaries at sea but not on land, where there was more to see
They wrote too many letters home
quiz.explanation: Sailors wrote diaries with only sky and sea to see, while land travellers, surrounded by things to observe, usually did not.

cards.title: Let decisions be tossed by argument before they are tossed by events
cards.body:
Bacon says the wisest leaders lose nothing by relying on advice. Every important matter, he argues, will be shaken up one way or another. Either it is tested in discussion with good advisers first, or it will be tested later by events, with all the doing and undoing of someone staggering home drunk.

He also gives two marks of bad advice: it comes from the inexperienced, and it pushes for something violent or extreme. Before a big decision, invite challenge. It is far cheaper to have your plan knocked around in a meeting than in reality.
cards.quote: if they be not tossed upon the arguments of counsel, they will be tossed upon the waves of fortune; and be full of inconstancy, doing and undoing, like the reeling of a drunken man.
cards.apply_it: Before your next important decision, ask one experienced person to argue against it for ten minutes.

quiz.question: What two marks of bad counsel does Bacon give?
options: It is written down and public
It comes from friends and family
quiz.explanation: From the story of Solomon's son, bad counsel is best known as young counsel for the person and violent counsel for the matter.

cards.title: Watch carefully at the start, then move fast once you commit
cards.body:
Bacon compares opportunity to a market: sometimes waiting brings the price down, but sometimes the chance shrinks while you hesitate. He says there is no greater wisdom than timing the start of things well.

His rule is to begin great actions like Argus, the mythical giant with a hundred eyes, and finish them like Briareus, who had a hundred hands. In other words, watch closely, then act with speed. Spend real time understanding a situation and choosing your moment. Once you decide, stop deliberating and execute quickly.
cards.quote: it is good, to commit the beginnings of all great actions to Argus, with his hundred eyes, and the ends to Briareus, with his hundred hands; first to watch, and then to speed.
cards.apply_it: For a decision you are sitting on, set a deadline for watching and gathering facts. After that date, switch fully to action.

quiz.question: What does Bacon mean by giving beginnings to Argus and endings to Briareus?
options: Watch closely first, then act quickly
quiz.explanation: Argus had a hundred eyes and Briareus a hundred hands: first to watch, and then to speed.

cards.title: Make big changes the way time does: steadily and almost unnoticed
cards.body:
Bacon sees both sides of change. New ideas are awkward at first and stir up resistance, while old customs fit together even when they are not good. But he insists that refusing all change is just as disruptive, because time itself keeps changing things. If wisdom does not change them for the better, time will change them for the worse.

His advice is to innovate like time does: greatly, but by degrees so small they are hardly noticed. In a workplace or family, that means steady, gradual improvement rather than dramatic overhauls that create winners and losers overnight.
cards.quote: Surely every medicine is an innovation; and he that will not apply new remedies, must expect new evils; for time is the greatest innovator
cards.apply_it: Pick one change you want to make at work or home. Break it into a small first step you can introduce this week.

quiz.question: How does Bacon think innovation is best done?
options: Never, because custom is always better
Gradually, by degrees, as time itself changes things
quiz.explanation: He advises following time, 'which indeed innovateth greatly, but quietly, by degrees scarce to be perceived'.

cards.title: Rushing to look fast is the slowest way to finish
cards.body:
Bacon warns that fake speed is one of the most dangerous things in business. It is like bolting food: it leaves you with problems later. He advises measuring progress by how far the work has actually advanced, not by how long you sat in meetings or how quickly you declared something done.

He quotes a wise friend who, seeing people hurry toward a conclusion, would say: wait a little, so we can finish sooner. Shortening a task by condensing it is good; shortening it by cutting corners only means doing it again later.
cards.quote: I knew a wise man that had it for a byword, when he saw men hasten to a conclusion, Stay a little, that we may make an end the sooner.
cards.apply_it: Next time you feel pressure to wrap something up fast, ask: what would we have to redo later if we skip this step?

quiz.question: How does Bacon say speed in business should be measured?
options: By how far the business actually advances
By how quickly decisions are announced
By how many people are involved
quiz.explanation: 'Measure not dispatch, by the times of sitting, but by the advancement of the business.'

cards.title: Let people tell it their way; interrupting makes it take longer
cards.body:
When someone is giving you the first account of a problem, Bacon advises listening well. If you need to steer them, do it at the start rather than cutting in halfway. Someone knocked out of their own order goes backwards and forwards, searching their memory, and ends up taking longer than if you had let them carry on.

He adds a dry note: sometimes the person running the meeting is more trouble than the speaker. Good chairs and good listeners set the direction early, then let people finish.
cards.quote: Give good hearing to those, that give the first information in business; and rather direct them in the beginning, than interrupt them in the continuance of their speeches
cards.apply_it: In your next conversation where someone explains a problem, agree on what you need at the start, then do not interrupt until they finish.

quiz.question: Why does Bacon advise against interrupting someone mid-explanation?
options: It is rude to their family
They lose their order and become more tedious
It makes the listener look foolish
quiz.explanation: A speaker put out of their own order goes forward and backward and becomes more tedious.

cards.title: A true friend is the only remedy that opens a heavy heart
cards.body:
Bacon lists the medicines of his day for opening up various organs, then says that nothing opens the heart except a true friend. The first fruit of friendship, he writes, is relief from the fullness and pressure that strong feelings create.

To a friend you can bring griefs, joys, fears, hopes, suspicions and anything else weighing on you, like a kind of confession. Feelings kept bottled up tend to grow heavier. Saying them to someone who cares does not solve every problem, but it eases the pressure in a way nothing else can.
cards.quote: no receipt openeth the heart, but a true friend; to whom you may impart griefs, joys, fears, hopes, suspicions, counsels, and whatsoever lieth upon the heart to oppress it
cards.apply_it: Think of what is weighing on you most right now. Message one friend and ask if they have time to talk this week.

quiz.question: What does Bacon say is the only thing that 'openeth the heart'?
quiz.explanation: He says no medicine opens the heart, 'but a true friend'.

cards.title: Explaining your thoughts to someone makes you wiser than an hour alone
cards.body:
Bacon's second fruit of friendship is clearer thinking. When your head is full of tangled ideas, talking them through with another person sorts them. You toss them around, put them in order, and see how they look in words. He says you become wiser than yourself, more in an hour's talk than in a day's thinking alone.

This is why explaining a topic to a study partner works so well. Even if they cannot advise you, the act of explaining sharpens your own understanding, like a knife on a whetstone that does not cut itself.
cards.quote: he waxeth wiser than himself; and that more by an hour's discourse, than by a day's meditation.
cards.apply_it: Pick a topic you are learning. Explain it out loud to a friend, or even to an empty chair, in five minutes, and note where you get stuck.

quiz.question: According to Bacon, why does talking through your thoughts help even if the listener gives no advice?
options: Putting thoughts into words orders and clarifies them
quiz.explanation: He says a man 'bringeth his own thoughts to light, and whetteth his wits as against a stone, which itself cuts not'.

cards.title: You are your own biggest flatterer, so you need a friend who tells the truth
cards.body:
Bacon says the advice we give ourselves is soaked in our own feelings and habits. Advice from an honest friend is 'drier', clearer and purer. The difference is as big as the difference between a friend and a flatterer, because no flatterer is as skilled as a person flattering themselves.

He notes how many serious mistakes people make simply because no one was free to point them out. The cure is a friend who has the liberty to tell you hard truths, and the willingness on your side to hear them.
cards.quote: For there is no such flatterer as is a man's self; and there is no such remedy against flattery of a man's self, as the liberty of a friend.
cards.apply_it: Ask one trusted friend: 'What is something about me you think I don't see?' Listen without defending yourself.

quiz.question: What does Bacon say is the best remedy against flattering yourself?
options: The freedom of an honest friend
quiz.explanation: He calls self-accounting too harsh and books too flat; the best remedy is the liberty of a friend.

cards.title: To stay steady, spend half your income; to grow wealthy, spend a third
cards.body:
Bacon says ordinary spending should be kept within your means and ordered so that your actual bills are lower than people might guess. He gives a rule of thumb: if you only want to stay even, keep regular expenses to half of what comes in. If you want to grow richer, keep them to a third.

Those ratios may be hard today, but the principle holds: wealth comes from the gap between earning and spending, set deliberately. He also says no one is too important to look at their own accounts. Some avoid it because they fear what they will find, but wounds cannot be cured without examining them.
cards.quote: Certainly, if a man will keep but of even hand, his ordinary expenses ought to be but to the half of his receipts; and if he think to wax rich, but to the third part.
cards.apply_it: Look at last month's spending and work out what share of your income it was. Pick one category to trim.

quiz.question: What share of income does Bacon suggest spending if you want to grow rich?
quiz.explanation: Half keeps you even; a third lets you 'wax rich'.

cards.title: Be wary of costs that keep coming back, and clear debt step by step
cards.body:
Bacon gives three practical money lessons. First, if you are generous in one kind of spending, be thrifty in another; spending freely on everything leads to ruin. Second, when getting out of debt, going too fast can hurt as much as going too slow. Clearing it gradually builds a habit of thrift, while clearing it all at once often leads to relapse.

Third, be careful about starting costs that will continue once begun, but be more relaxed with one-off expenses. Today that means thinking twice about every subscription and recurring commitment.
cards.quote: A man ought warily to begin charges which once begun will continue; but in matters that return not, he may be more magnificent.
cards.apply_it: List every recurring payment you have. Cancel one you would not sign up for today.

quiz.question: Why does Bacon prefer clearing debts gradually rather than all at once?
options: Gradual clearing builds a lasting habit of frugality
quiz.explanation: He says whoever clears all at once tends to relapse, while clearing by degrees 'induceth a habit of frugality'.

cards.title: Your own observation of what helps and harms you is valuable health knowledge
cards.body:
Bacon begins his essay on health with a point beyond formal medicine: noticing what does you good and what does you harm is one of the best ways to stay well. He adds a careful rule. It is safer to say 'this does not agree with me, so I will stop' than 'this has not hurt me yet, so it is fine'. Youth, he notes, can carry excesses that get charged back later.

Today that might mean paying attention to how certain foods, screen time or late nights leave you feeling, alongside, not instead of, professional advice.
cards.quote: a man's own observation, what he finds good of, and what he finds hurt of, is the best physic to preserve health.
cards.apply_it: For one week, jot down one thing each day that left you feeling better and one that left you feeling worse.

quiz.question: Which conclusion does Bacon consider safer?
options: 'This hasn't hurt me, so I can keep using it'
'Young people need not worry about health'
'This doesn't agree with me, so I'll stop it'
quiz.explanation: He says it is safer to stop what disagrees with you than to assume something is fine because it has not hurt you yet.

cards.title: Change health habits gradually, and adjust as you get older
cards.body:
Bacon advises noticing when you are getting older and not expecting to do the same things forever: age will not be defied. He suggests examining your habits of diet, sleep, exercise and clothing, and dropping any harmful one little by little. If a change causes problems, go back and try again.

He also warns against sudden big changes in one area without adjusting the rest. Small, steady adjustments that you can monitor tend to stick better than dramatic overhauls. Always talk to a health professional about significant changes.
cards.quote: Discern of the coming on of years, and think not to do the same things still; for age will not be defied.
cards.apply_it: Choose one habit you would like to change and make a small first adjustment this week, then check how you feel.

quiz.question: How does Bacon recommend dropping a harmful habit?
options: Little by little, returning if the change causes trouble
By replacing it with a stronger habit
quiz.explanation: He says to discontinue it 'by little and little', coming back to it if the change brings inconvenience.

cards.title: A cheerful mind at meals, sleep and exercise helps you last
cards.body:
Bacon believed mood matters for long life. Being relaxed and cheerful at mealtimes, at bedtime and during exercise is, he says, one of the best rules for lasting well.

He lists states of mind to avoid: envy, anxious fears, anger that eats inward, sadness not shared with anyone, and excess of any kind. And he lists ones to welcome: hope, gentle mirth rather than wild joy, variety of pleasures, wonder, and reading that fills the mind with bright things such as history, stories and nature. If low mood or worry persists, reaching out to someone is part of good health, not a failure of it.
cards.quote: To be free-minded and cheerfully disposed, at hours of meat, and of sleep, and of exercise, is one of the best precepts of long lasting.
cards.apply_it: Tonight, leave worries and screens away from one meal or your last half-hour before sleep.

quiz.question: Which of these does Bacon list as something to avoid for good health?
quiz.explanation: He advises against 'sadness not communicated' and recommends hopes, mirth and wonder instead.

cards.title: Suspicion grows in the dark; the cure is to find out more
cards.body:
Bacon compares suspicions to bats: they fly at twilight. They cloud the mind, cost you friends and slow everything down. They make leaders tyrants and partners jealous. And the main thing that feeds suspicion, he says, is knowing too little.

His remedies are practical. Find out more instead of brooding. Plan as if the suspicion might be true, so it cannot hurt you, while treating it as false in how you behave. Often the best step is to raise it openly with the person concerned, which clears the air and makes them more careful.
cards.quote: There is nothing makes a man suspect much, more than to know little; and therefore men should remedy suspicion, by procuring to know more, and not to keep their suspicions in smother.
cards.apply_it: If you are quietly suspicious of someone, write down what you actually know. Then decide on one calm question you could ask them.

quiz.question: According to Bacon, what most causes suspicion?
quiz.explanation: He says nothing makes a man suspect more than knowing little, so the remedy is to learn more.

cards.title: The best talker starts topics, varies them and lets others have the floor
cards.body:
Bacon says some people talk to show off how clever they are, arguing any side, rather than to work out what is true. Others have a few pet topics and wear them out. The most honourable part of conversation, he says, is to open a subject, guide it and move on to something else.

He suggests mixing stories with reasons, questions with opinions, and jokes with serious points. And make sure others get their turn; if someone hogs the conversation, find a way to bring others in, like musicians cutting short a dancer who goes on too long.
cards.quote: The honorablest part of talk, is to give the occasion; and again to moderate, and pass to somewhat else; for then a man leads the dance.
cards.apply_it: In your next group conversation, ask one quieter person a question that invites them in.

quiz.question: What does Bacon call the 'honorablest part of talk'?
options: Opening a topic, guiding it and moving on
quiz.explanation: To give the occasion, moderate and pass to something else is to 'lead the dance'.

cards.title: Know the difference between wit and cruelty
cards.body:
Bacon says humour has its limits. Some subjects deserve to be off-limits for jokes, including any situation that deserves pity. He urges people to learn the difference between 'saltness', lively wit that adds flavour, and 'bitterness', jokes that wound.

His warning for the sharp-tongued is worth remembering: if your wit makes others afraid of you, you had better be afraid of their memory. People forget clever lines but remember being made to feel small. A good host, he notes, makes sure no guest leaves feeling mocked.
cards.quote: Certainly, he that hath a satirical vein, as he maketh others afraid of his wit, so he had need be afraid of others' memory.
cards.apply_it: Before your next teasing remark, ask: would this still be funny if it were said about me, in front of people I respect?

quiz.question: What does Bacon warn people with a satirical, cutting wit?
quiz.explanation: Those who make others afraid of their wit 'had need be afraid of others' memory'.

cards.title: Earn money fairly, use it soberly, share it gladly, leave it calmly
cards.body:
Bacon calls riches the 'baggage of virtue': you cannot do without it, but it slows the march. He says great wealth has no real use to its owner beyond giving it out; the rest is mostly a feeling of importance. Yet he also warns against pretending to despise money.

His summary is a fine guide for a whole financial life. Seek only wealth you can earn honestly. Use it with moderation. Share it cheerfully. And be able to let it go without bitterness. He adds a warning against hurrying after riches, since quick money often comes by unjust means.
cards.quote: Seek not proud riches, but such as thou mayest get justly, use soberly, distribute cheerfully, and leave contentedly.
cards.apply_it: Write down one way you could use money more generously this month, even in a small amount.

quiz.question: What does Bacon call riches?
quiz.explanation: Like an army's baggage, riches cannot be left behind but they hinder the march.

cards.title: Aim to excel at a few great things, not to be seen in everything
cards.body:
Bacon compares two kinds of ambition. Wanting to succeed at important things is less harmful than wanting to appear in everything, which only breeds confusion and spoils work. Wanting to stand out among capable people is a hard task, but it is good for everyone. Wanting to be the only star among nobodies damages a whole generation.

The lesson for a modern career is to choose a few things worth doing really well, and to seek out strong peers rather than weak ones to shine against.
cards.quote: He that seeketh to be eminent amongst able men, hath a great task; but that is ever good for the public. But he, that plots to be the only figure amongst ciphers, is the decay of a whole age.
cards.apply_it: List the projects you are involved in. Which one or two deserve your best effort, and which could you step back from?

quiz.question: Which kind of ambition does Bacon call 'the decay of a whole age'?
options: Plotting to be the only figure among ciphers
Seeking to be eminent among able people
quiz.explanation: Standing out among able people is good for all; being the only star among nobodies corrupts an age.

cards.title: Set yourself tasks that are hard but not crushing, and practise harder than the real thing
cards.body:
Bacon says our nature is often hidden, sometimes overcome, but seldom wiped out. Only steady habit truly changes it. If you want to change something in yourself, don't set tasks so big you keep failing and lose heart, or so small you barely progress.

Start with help, the way swimmers once used floats. Later practise with handicaps, as dancers trained in heavy shoes. He notes that practice harder than the real thing builds great skill. And sometimes take a break: constant practice without pause can fix your mistakes in place along with your skills.
cards.quote: For it breeds great perfection, if the practice be harder than the use.
cards.apply_it: Pick one skill or habit you are building. Adjust this week's goal so it is challenging but achievable.

quiz.question: Why does Bacon warn against setting yourself too great a task?
options: Frequent failure will make you lose heart
quiz.explanation: Too great a task makes a person 'dejected by often failings'; too small makes slow progress.

cards.title: People do what they are used to doing, not what they promise
cards.body:
Bacon makes a sharp observation: our thoughts follow our inclinations, our words follow what we have learned, but our actions follow our habits. That is why you can hear people make bold promises and then do exactly what they did before, as if run by the wheels of habit.

Since habit is, as he puts it, the chief ruler of a person's life, the real work is to build good habits. Resolutions and speeches are not enough. If you want different results, change the small things you repeat every day.
cards.quote: Men's thoughts, are much according to their inclination; their discourse and speeches, according to their learning and infused opinions; but their deeds, are after as they have been accustomed.
cards.apply_it: Choose one promise you have made yourself more than once. Turn it into a tiny daily action you can repeat tomorrow.

quiz.question: According to Bacon, what mostly governs people's deeds?
quiz.explanation: Thoughts follow inclination, speech follows learning, but deeds follow custom.

cards.title: Luck matters, but much of your fortune is shaped by your own hands
cards.body:
Bacon admits that outside events, such as favour, opportunity and others' mistakes, shape success. But mainly, he says, the mould of a person's fortune is in their own hands.

He compares good fortune to the Milky Way: a band of light made of many small stars, too faint to see one by one but bright together. In the same way, many small, hardly noticed habits and qualities add up to what looks like luck. He also says that if you look sharply and attentively, you can see fortune: she is blind, but not invisible.
cards.quote: The way of fortune, is like the Milken Way in the sky; which is a meeting or knot of a number of small stars; not seen asunder, but giving light together.
cards.apply_it: List three small habits that have quietly helped your life so far. Which one could you strengthen?

quiz.question: What does Bacon compare the way of fortune to?
options: The Milky Way, made of many small stars
quiz.explanation: Many small, scarcely noticed virtues together create what looks like good fortune.

cards.title: Mix young and old on a team; each corrects the other's faults
cards.body:
Bacon gives a frank list. Young people take on more than they can handle, rush to the end without thinking through the steps, try extreme fixes first and won't admit mistakes. Older people object too much, consult too long, risk too little, regret too quickly and settle for average results.

His answer is to combine them. The strengths of each age correct the weaknesses of the other, the young learn while the experienced lead, and the team gets both authority and energy. It is an early case for mixed-age teams.
cards.quote: Men of age object too much, consult too long, adventure too little, repent too soon, and seldom drive business home to the full period, but content themselves with a mediocrity of success.
cards.apply_it: Whatever your age, ask someone from a different generation for their view on a current problem.

quiz.question: What does Bacon recommend about young and older people in work?
options: Combine them so each corrects the other
quiz.explanation: He says it is good to 'compound employments of both', since each age's virtues correct the other's defects.

cards.title: Talk in person for delicate matters; write when you need a record
cards.body:
Bacon says it is usually better to deal by speech than by letter. Writing is useful when you want a written reply, a record to justify yourself later, or when you might be interrupted. But face-to-face works best in delicate situations, because watching the other person's expression tells you how far to go.

He ends with advice for any hard negotiation: you cannot sow and reap at once. Prepare the ground and let agreement ripen in stages. The same applies to emails versus calls today.
cards.quote: In all negotiations of difficulty, a man may not look to sow and reap at once; but must prepare business, and so ripen it by degrees.
cards.apply_it: For your next sensitive conversation, choose a call or meeting over email, and aim only for the first step, not the final yes.

quiz.question: Why does Bacon favour meeting in person for delicate matters?
options: You can read the other person's face to judge how far to go
quiz.explanation: In tender cases, a man's eye on the other's face 'may give him a direction how far to go'.

cards.title: Some books are for tasting, some for swallowing, a few for chewing
cards.body:
In his most famous essay, Bacon says not to read in order to argue, nor to believe everything, nor just to have something to say, but to weigh and consider.

He sorts books into three kinds. Some are worth only a taste: read in parts. Some can be swallowed: read through, but not closely. And a few must be chewed and digested: read completely, with full attention. Matching your reading style to the book saves time and gives your best focus to what deserves it.
cards.quote: Some books are to be tasted, others to be swallowed, and some few to be chewed and digested
cards.apply_it: Sort your current reading list into taste, swallow and chew. Give the 'chew' book your best hour of the day.

quiz.question: What does Bacon mean by books that are 'chewed and digested'?
options: Books read wholly, with diligence and attention
quiz.explanation: Some few books are 'to be read wholly, and with diligence and attention'.

cards.title: Reading fills you, discussion sharpens you, writing makes you precise
cards.body:
Bacon sums up three ways of learning in one line. Reading makes a full person, stocked with knowledge. Conversation makes a ready person, quick to respond. Writing makes an exact person, careful and precise.

He adds that each covers for the others: if you write little you need a great memory, if you discuss little you need quick wits. For students today, this is a strong case for mixing methods. Read the material, talk it over with others, and write it out in your own words.
cards.quote: Reading maketh a full man; conference a ready man; and writing an exact man.
cards.apply_it: After your next study session, spend five minutes writing a summary from memory, and explain it to someone later.

quiz.question: According to Bacon, what does writing make a person?
quiz.explanation: Reading makes a full man, conference a ready man, and writing an exact man.

cards.title: Popularity floats light things to the top and sinks heavy ones
cards.body:
Bacon warns that praise from the crowd is often unreliable. It tends to follow showy people more than truly good ones, because the deepest virtues are hard for most people to see.

His image is striking: fame is like a river that carries light, swollen things on the surface and drowns the weighty and solid. In an age of viral content, it is worth remembering. What gets the most attention is not necessarily what is most valuable. Praise from people of real judgment, he says, lasts much longer.
cards.quote: Certainly fame is like a river, that beareth up things light and swoln, and drowns things weighty and solid.
cards.apply_it: Think of whose approval you seek most. Is it the crowd's, or the judgment of a few people you truly respect?

quiz.question: What does Bacon compare fame to?
options: A river that carries light things and drowns heavy ones
quiz.explanation: Fame bears up things 'light and swoln' and drowns things 'weighty and solid'.

cards.title: Don't try to never be angry; keep anger short and contained
cards.body:
Bacon thinks trying to wipe out anger completely is just Stoic bravado. Instead he quotes older advice: be angry, but do not do wrong, and do not let the sun go down on your anger. Anger should be limited both in how far it goes and how long it lasts.

To calm a quick temper over time, he suggests reflecting on what anger does to your life, and the best moment for that is after the fit has fully passed. Looking back calmly at a recent outburst teaches more than any resolution made in the heat of it.
cards.quote: Anger must be limited and confined, both in race and in time.
cards.apply_it: After your next moment of anger has passed, take two minutes to note what triggered it and what it cost you.

quiz.question: When does Bacon say is the best time to reflect on anger?
options: When the fit is completely over
quiz.explanation: He says the best time is 'to look back upon anger, when the fit is thoroughly over'.

cards.title: Anger burns hottest when you read contempt into an injury
cards.body:
Bacon names three main causes of anger. First, being very sensitive to hurt. Second, interpreting the hurt as a sign of contempt: the sense of being disrespected sharpens anger even more than the harm itself. Third, feeling that your reputation has been touched.

His remedy for the last is to have a 'thicker cloth of honour', a less fragile sense of pride. Above all, he says, win time. Tell yourself the moment to respond has not yet come. Often the anger fades before you need to act.
cards.quote: for contempt is that, which putteth an edge upon anger, as much or more than the hurt itself.
cards.apply_it: Next time you feel slighted, ask: is the harm itself serious, or is it the feeling of being disrespected? Wait an hour before replying.

quiz.question: Which cause does Bacon say sharpens anger as much as or more than the hurt itself?
quiz.explanation: The perception of contempt 'putteth an edge upon anger, as much or more than the hurt itself'.

cards.title: Whatever you feel in anger, don't say the unforgivable or do the irreversible
cards.body:
Bacon accepts that anger will sometimes take hold. His concern is to keep it from causing lasting damage. He names two cautions.

First, avoid extremely bitter, cutting words, especially personal ones that hit exactly where it hurts, and never reveal secrets in anger. Second, don't break off any relationship or deal in a fit of temper. You may show you are upset, but do nothing that cannot be undone. Arguments end; resignation letters, ended friendships and shared secrets are harder to take back.
cards.quote: do not peremptorily break off, in any business, in a fit of anger; but howsoever you show bitterness, do not act anything, that is not revocable.
cards.apply_it: Make a personal rule: no quitting, ending or sending anything final while angry. Sleep on it first.

quiz.question: Which is one of Bacon's two cautions for containing anger?
options: Do nothing that cannot be undone
quiz.explanation: He advises showing bitterness if you must, but not acting 'anything, that is not revocable'.

cards.title: Choose a good moment to share bad news, and don't frame it as contempt
cards.body:
Bacon explains how anger is stirred in others: by catching them at a bad time, and by piling up details that make the injury look like an insult. The remedies are the opposite.

First, pick a good time to tell someone upsetting news, because first impressions matter a great deal. Second, separate the harm from any sense of contempt by putting it down to misunderstanding, fear or emotion. When delivering bad news or apologising, giving the charitable explanation helps people stay calm.
cards.quote: The former to take good times, when first to relate to a man an angry business; for the first impression is much
cards.apply_it: If you have difficult news to share, plan when the person will be most rested and least rushed.

quiz.question: What does Bacon suggest to stop an injury feeling like contempt?
options: Put it down to misunderstanding, fear or passion
quiz.explanation: He suggests severing the injury from contempt, 'imputing it to misunderstanding, fear, passion, or what you will'.
